page: Amazon Web Services m4.2xlarge is a fourth-generation general-purpose virtual instance operating on the Xen hypervisor. It is powered by an x86_64 Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 processor operating at a base clock speed of 2.4 GHz. Hardware allocation includes 8 dedicated vCPUs derived from 4 physical cores via multithreading, supported by 32 KB of L1 data cache per core, 0.25 MB of L2 cache, and a shared 45 MB L3 cache. Memory capacity is 32.0 GB, maintaining a standard 1:4 vCPU-to-memory ratio. The instance provisions no integrated local storage and includes a 1 Gbps baseline network throughput. Discrete GPU accelerators are not present.

Benchmark evaluations reveal performance traits characteristic of the Broadwell processor family. Single-threaded capability sits in the lower percentile ranges, as reflected by a Geekbench single-core score of 973.0 and a single-core stress-ng result of 1263.99. Multithreaded execution achieves mid-tier levels, demonstrated by a multi-core stress-ng mark of 6290.33 and a Passmark CPU score of 7007.9. Uncached memory throughput sustains 46.46 GB/sec for 256 MB reads and 34.84 GB/sec for writes. Vector instruction capability is constrained to AVX2, with no support for modern AVX-512 or AMX instruction extensions.

The primary operational tradeoff centers on reliance on network-attached storage coupled with a modest 1 Gbps baseline networking pipe. In qualitative cost-efficiency terms, the hardware provides steady multi-core execution and predictable memory density, but offers reduced compute per cycle compared to newer architectures. The instance is suited for general enterprise application backends, legacy software compilation pipelines, microservices, and moderate batch processing that do not demand fast local I/O or advanced vector acceleration.
description: Amazon Web Services m4.2xlarge is a general-purpose virtual instance based on the Xen hypervisor, powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 processor operating at 2.4 GHz. The configuration allocates 8 dedicated vCPUs across 4 physical cores alongside 32.0 GB of memory, preserving a standard 1:4 vCPU-to-memory ratio. It features no local NVMe storage and operates with a 1 Gbps baseline network capacity without GPU acceleration. Across synthetic benchmarks, single-thread processing reflects the legacy microarchitecture, yielding lower-quartile scores such as a Geekbench single-core mark of 973.0. In contrast, multi-core metrics like the Passmark CPU score of 7007.9 and memory bandwidth reaching 46.46 GB/sec for large uncached reads fall within mid-range percentiles. Lacking modern AVX-512 extensions and local disks, this instance is appropriate for standard business applications, legacy software builds, low-traffic web backends, and moderate batch processing tasks where baseline network throughput and steady multithreaded capacity are sufficient.
